## Statement of Purpose
The purpose of this project is to predict and explain the rise in consumer debt over the past 20 years. The goal is to not only understand the underlying trends, but also to analyze the macroeconomic and political factors driving the rise in consumer debt. Understanding the main contributing factors responsible for rising consumer debt can help us better address this problem and to help lower the total debt or at least slow the rate at which it is accumulated.  

## Executive Summary
From the models I tested, the multiple linear regression model with predictors from best subset selection is the best-performing model in predicting total consumer debt, having the lowest prediction error, with a CV-RMSE of 0.410, compared to the Random Forest model with all predictors, a CV-RMSE of 0.709, and for the Single Linear Regression model, a CV-RMSE of 0.737. This suggests that a combination of economic and political factors have better predicting power than single predictors or more complex models than the random forest model. 

## Introduction
The data set contains 55 observations and 23 variables. The variable we aim to explain is total, which represents the total amount of consumer debt represented in trillions of dollars.

Please note that the is_recession variable is represented as 0's and 1's, where 0 represents no recession, and 1 represents a recession. A recession is defined as two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, a decline in consumer spending, a decline in consumer sentiment, and a rise in unemployment.

For the variables, pres_party, house_party, and senate_party, 0 represents Republican control and 1 represents Democrat control. Fiscal policy and government spending is influenced by political party control, which can influence consumer spending habits.

Names of the Features used in the Data Set: Most of the variable names here are self explanatory, but I'll give a basic explanation of some of the financial terms you may not be familiar with. HE (Home Equity) revolving debt is where you borrow against your home and use it to pay for goods and services. It is a secured type of debt that uses your home as collateral. The average CPI (Consumer Price Index) is used to track the average changes in cost of living. The effective federal funds rate is the baseline interest rate for borrowing costs set by the Federal Reserve.

Summary of the Data Set: This is a nice overview of the numerical values in the data set. The total consumer debt covers a wide range, from 7.38 to 18.78 trillion dollars, a massive figure. You can see the mortgage debt makes up a large portion of that amount, ranging from 5.08 to 13.17 trillion. 
For interest rates, the effective federal funds rate is relatively small when compared to the other interest rates, but increases from 0.07% to 5.26%, a nearly 75 times increase. The data follows a positive linear trend, so I only include the minimum, maximum, and median values. The values are represented in trillions of dollars. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
```
```{r}
lr_train |>
  arrange(date) |>
  summarize(
    min_debt = min(total),
    max_debt = max(total),
    median_debt = median(total)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = "Metric",
               values_to = "Value") |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

Here is a better representation of consumer debt over time. This shows the rate of change for total consumer debt on a quarterly basis. The growth over time stays relatively consistent where the max surge is likely caused by periods of financial stress, such as the recessions in 2008 and 2020. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
lr_train |> 
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(debt_growth = (total - lag(total)) / lag(total) * 100) |>
  summarize(
    avg_growth = mean(debt_growth, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_surge = max(debt_growth, na.rm = TRUE),
    volatility = sd(debt_growth, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = "Metric",
               values_to = "Value") |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

Here we can see the rise in total consumer debt over time. We can see a decline after the 2008 housing market crash, which would be the result in delinquencies following that crisis. After that, there is a steady rise in consumer debt following the event, and sharper rise following 2020, a result of the events that took place during COVID-19. 
What's interesting is that there is a sharp rise in debt before the housing market crash in 2008, which closely resembles the sharp rise in debt following COVID-19 in 2020. Whether this implies an upcoming recession is up for debate, but it is worth noting considering recent events. I go into further detail below in my EDA, as well as in my conclusion.


Below we can see consumer debt broken down into their individual categories. Mortgage debt is significantly larger than any other category, which isn't surprising considering recent home valuations. Following mortgage debt, we have auto and student loans as well as credit card debt, which over the past 3-4 years has been growing at a faster pace. This would be a result of the increase in the effective federal funds rate and rise in inflation, which is discussed further below.

Payments for student loans were paused during COVID-19 and resumed around 2023. Many are struggling to pay off their student loans due to a lack of job opportunities in a slowing job market.

Here we look at the total consumer debt and the growth rate in consumer debt in relation to whether or not the economy is expanding or contracting. We can see higher debt levels during times of economic expansion, which makes sense as consumers typically spend more during times of growth when compared to times of economic contraction and uncertainty. It's worth noting that data points during a recession are far fewer when compared to data points I have during times of economic expansion. That being said, it's a nice graphical representation of debt expanding and contracting as shown below. We can see debt in its expansion phase has an upward trend, with far more outliers on the high side.

## Model Selection Process
I decided to run best subset first to find the best combination of predictors for my model. We can see that the predictors on line 7 are the best combination here: unemployment_rate, cpi_index_avg, personal_savings_rate, is_recession, house_party, mortgage rate, and effective federal funds rate. 
I'm surprised the credit card interest rate didn't make the cut here, though it is tied to the effective federal funds (EFF) rate, so using it may be redundant. That being said, mortgage rate is being included, indicating that even if it is tied to the EFF rate, the fact that mortgage debt makes up a very large portion of consumer debt, it is a significant predictor for total consumer debt.  What's more surprising is that house party seemed to be an important predictor in total consumer debt, while the senate and presidential party are not. This is most likely because the House house the power of initiating spending bills, which may have impact on consumer spending. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
best_model <- regsubsets(total ~ consumer_sentiment + unemployment_rate + cc_interest_rate + cpi_index_avg + personal_savings_rate 
                      + is_recession + pres_party + house_party + senate_party + hiring_rate + job_turnover_rate + mortgage_rate
                      + eff_fed_funds_rate + auto_loan_rate, data = lr_train, nvmax = 14)
res_sum <- summary(best_model)
res_sum$outmat
which.min(res_sum$bic)
```

This is a visual representation of the best subset, where the top line shows which predictors carry the most weight in predicting total consumer debt. Note that the black boxes indicate useful predictors and white boxes indicate those that are not.
```{r}
#| echo: false
plot(best_model, scale = "bic") 
```

Having used the best subset selection it is worth noting that the data set I have is fairly small, with only 23 variables and 55 observations, so the risk of overfitting is high. Using LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) we can identify and drop predictors that don't add any value to my model. We can see that a model with 7 predictors has the best predictive power without an overly complex model. 
For clarification LASSO works by adding a penalty to the model for each predictor included. It acts as a budget for the model, limiting the amount 'spent' on predictors, forcing the least useful ones out by forcing its coefficient down to zero. This helps clear out the 'noise' from our data set, making sure only the useful predictors stay. Before the penalty is applied, the predictors are standardized, so predictors on different scales are treated fairly. We use cv.glmnet() for this, where standardize argument is set to TRUE by default. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
x_train <- model.matrix(total ~ consumer_sentiment + unemployment_rate + cc_interest_rate + 
                        cpi_index_avg + personal_savings_rate + is_recession + 
                        pres_party + house_party + senate_party + hiring_rate + 
                        job_turnover_rate + mortgage_rate + eff_fed_funds_rate + 
                        auto_loan_rate, data = lr_train)[,-1]
y_train <- lr_train$total
set.seed(123) # For reproducibility
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1) # cv.glmnet uses standardize, which is TRUE by default. Standardizes predictors
plot(cv_lasso)
```

We can see that the LASSO method dropped unemployment rate, credit card interest rate, job turnover rate, mortgage rate, presidential party, and auto loan as predictors. Comparing the two models, there is a difference in the selection of predictors. In the LASSO method, unemployment and mortgage rate are dropped, but keeps consumer sentiment, senate party and hiring rate. Best Subset keeps unemployment rate and mortgage rate, but drops senate party, consumer sentiment and hiring rate as predictors. Both methods agree on average CPI, effective federal funds rate, personal savings rate, recession, and house party as predictors. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
best_lambda <- cv_lasso$lambda.min
lasso_coefs <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min")
print(lasso_coefs) 
```

This is an evaluation on the LASSO models performance on the test data. We can see the RMSE is roughly 0.459, suggesting this model is off by about $459 billion. I use these predictors below in my multiple linear regression model and random forest model below and discuss the results further in my interpretation of the models. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
x_test <- model.matrix(total ~ consumer_sentiment + unemployment_rate + cc_interest_rate + 
                       cpi_index_avg + personal_savings_rate + is_recession + 
                       pres_party + house_party + senate_party + hiring_rate + 
                       job_turnover_rate + mortgage_rate + eff_fed_funds_rate + 
                       auto_loan_rate, data = lr_test)[,-1]
lasso_preds <- predict(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min", newx = x_test)
rmse_vec(lr_test$total, as.vector(lasso_preds)) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

## Linear Regression Model Construction with Single Predictor 
Below I have my linear regression model with a single predictor. I use average consumer price index of all consumer goods and services to explain total consumer debt over time. This explains roughly 90% of total consumer debt, which makes sense since they are highly correlated. That being said, it isn't the only predictor of consumer debt, as I'll show in my multiple linear regression model below.
```{r}
#| echo: false
lin_reg_fl_spec <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm")
lin_reg_fl_rec <- recipe(total ~ cpi_index_avg, data = lr_train) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |> #handles missing values
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |> #handles new data
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> #change to numeric columns
  step_zv(all_predictors()) #remove predictor variables that contain only a single value
lin_reg_fl_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lin_reg_fl_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lin_reg_fl_rec)
lin_reg_fl_fit <- lin_reg_fl_wf |>
  fit(lr_train)
glance(lin_reg_fl_fit) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

Here we see how well the model generalizes by predicting the consumer debt for the test set and computing standard regression metrics such as RMSE and R squared. The RMSE shows we are off by about $877 billion.
```{r}
#| echo: false
slr_test_aug <- augment(lin_reg_fl_fit, new_data = lr_test)

slr_test_aug |>
  metrics(truth = total, estimate = .pred) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

Here is a reassessment of the single linear regression model using cross-validation. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
slr_res <- fit_resamples(
  lin_reg_fl_wf,
  resamples = rf_debt_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

collect_metrics(slr_res) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

## Linear Regression Model Construction with Multiple Predictors from Best Subset Selection
Below is the linear regression model with multiple predictors picked from the best subset selection process. Below the results here I have a separate model for the predictors chosen with the LASSO method. The improvement in performance of this model is significant, having nearly half the score in AIC, suggesting this model is the better choice over the single linear regression model. The adjusted r-squared value explains nearly 98% of the variance in the data points. The deviance from the regression line is far smaller as well, emphasizing the predictive power of this model. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
m_lin_reg_fl_spec <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm")

m_lin_reg_fl_rec <- recipe(total ~ unemployment_rate + cpi_index_avg + personal_savings_rate + is_recession + 
                                   house_party + mortgage_rate + eff_fed_funds_rate, data = lr_train) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # Handles missing values
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # Handles new data
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>   # Change to numeric columns
  step_zv(all_predictors())

m_lin_reg_fl_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(m_lin_reg_fl_spec) |>
  add_recipe(m_lin_reg_fl_rec)
m_lin_reg_fl_fit <- m_lin_reg_fl_wf |>
  fit(lr_train)
glance(m_lin_reg_fl_fit) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

We see an improvement in the prediction error as well, validating my observation that the multiple linear regression model here is superior than the simple linear regression model. 
```{r}
#| echo: false

mlr_test_aug |>
  metrics(truth = total, estimate = .pred) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

Here is a reassessment of the multiple linear regression model using cross-validation
```{r}

  m_lin_reg_fl_wf,
  resamples = rf_debt_folds,

collect_metrics(mlr_res) |>

```

## Linear Regression Model Construction with Multiple Predictors from LASSO method
Here we have the multiple linear regression model with the predictors chosen using the LASSO method. The results are nearly identical. I will keep this here as a reference point and a reminder that reliance on a single model is not advised. As I stated before, the size of my data set is small, so there is a risk of overfitting. Having both models is helpful in analyzing new data and making future predictions. The metrics below suggest that the multiple linear regression model with best subset is preferred, according to AIC. 

## Random Forest Model Construction with all Predictors
Here we have a random forest model using all predictors. This model performs marginally better than the simple linear regression model, but fails to outperform the multiple linear regression model. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("regression")

rf_rec <- recipe(total ~ unemployment_rate + cpi_index_avg + consumer_sentiment + pres_party + auto_loan_rate +
                        personal_savings_rate + is_recession + cc_interest_rate + senate_party +
                        house_party + mortgage_rate + eff_fed_funds_rate + hiring_rate + job_turnover_rate, 
                        data = rf_train) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(rf_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rf_rec)
rf_res <- fit_resamples(
  rf_wf,
  resamples = rf_debt_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

collect_metrics(rf_res) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling()
```

With this model we can see that average CPI is the most important predictor, followed by credit card interest rate, which is interesting considering that both the best subset and LASSO method excluded credit card interest rate. This aligns with my intuition in thinking that credit card interest rate would play a role in predicting consumer debt, considering it sits at roughly 21%. Though credit card debt is not as large as the other types of debt, the high interest rate has compounding power, as I mentioned earlier in my report. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
final_rf_fit <- rf_wf |> 
  fit(data = rf_train)

final_rf_fit |> 
  extract_fit_parsnip() |> 
  vip(geom = "col", mapping = aes(fill = Importance)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "steelblue", high = "firebrick") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest Variable Importance with all Predictors",
       subtitle = "Key predictors of total consumer debt")
```

## Random Forest Model Construction with LASSO method
Here we see the random forest model with predictors from the LASSO method. This performed worse than all of the other models. This doesn't necessarily suggest that the predictors we used here are not useful, but may just indicate the random forest model is not a good fit for estimating the observed data and a less complex model would be best for estimating total consumer debt. 
```{r}

  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>

lasso_rf_rec <- recipe(total ~ cpi_index_avg + personal_savings_rate + is_recession + 
                         house_party + senate_party + eff_fed_funds_rate + hiring_rate,

  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

lasso_rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lasso_rf_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lasso_rf_rec)
lasso_rf_res <- fit_resamples(
  lasso_rf_wf,
  resamples = rf_debt_folds,

)

collect_metrics(lasso_rf_res) |>
```

## Model Performance Assessment
In this section, I reassess the three previously constructed models using 10-fold cross-validation. This provides a more robust estimate of how the models will perform on unseen data compared to the single validation split used in previous assignments. The multiple linear regression model outperforms the simple linear regression and the random forest model. The combination of predictors from the best subset selection used in multiple linear regression have high accuracy in predicting consumer debt. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
# Combines the results into one table
model_comparison <- bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(slr_res) |> mutate(model = "Simple Linear Regression"),
  collect_metrics(mlr_res) |> mutate(model = "Multiple Linear Regression"),
  collect_metrics(lasso_mlr_res) |> mutate(model = "LASSO MLR"),
  collect_metrics(rf_res)  |> mutate(model = "Random Forest"),
  collect_metrics(lasso_rf_res) |> mutate(model = "Lasso RF"),
  collect_metrics(bss_rf_res) |> mutate(model = "Best Subset Random Forest")
) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |> 
  select(model, mean, std_err) |>
  arrange(mean)

model_comparison |>
  kable(caption = "Cross-Validation Performance Comparison (RMSE)") |>
  kable_styling()
```

## Model Interpretation and Inference
The multiple linear regression model with predictors from best subset selection outperforms all other models, having the lowest prediction error. The multiple linear regression model with predictors from the LASSO method is a close second, followed by the random forest model with all predictors. Random forest models typically perform well, but the limited size of the data set may have impacted performance. It could also suggest that less complex models are better equipped in predicting total debt with the provided predictors. The random forest model with predictors from the LASSO method performed the worst out of all models. The complexity of this model may have contributed to its poor performance. 
 
## Conclusion
I'd like to point out that after extensively testing and training my models here, that unseen events could have a substantial impact on consumer debt levels that cannot be explained by my models here. Such events could include the current situation with oil supply constraints, which could lead to a cascading set of negative events that could lead to either a substantial rise in debt, or lead to delinquencies and defaults lowering the debt, but erasing capital throughout the economy. 
An issue I would like to point out with my model is the way the data is split for training and testing. In hindsight, I should have used the most recent data for testing and past data for training, which would have made for a more reliable model in terms of predictive power. Random splitting is standard for general regression, but time-series splitting (back testing) is preferred for economic forecasting to avoid 'look-ahead bias'. The proportion of data I used for training from the data set is 60%, which I believe to be a appropriate amount considering the size of the data set.
